y-m-33-01.title: Where did Seojin's calculation of (x−2)³ go wrong?
y-m-33-01.topic: Multiplication formula (expanding a cube) and checking for sign errors
y-m-33-01.goal: In a solution that applies the cube formula to an expression with a negative number, find the first line that went wrong, learn that checking by plugging in numbers can miss the error at some values, and test the corrected result yourself.
y-m-33-01.material: For homework, Seojin expanded (x−2)³ using the multiplication formula (a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ and wrote the solution in five lines. x is a letter standing for a real number, and −2 goes in the place of b in the formula. Seojin wants to submit the result of the 5th line as it is. Let's check whether we can trust that result. (How to read: x³ is 'x cubed', (−2)² is 'negative 2, squared', 3·x·(−4) is '3 times x times negative 4')
y-m-33-01.thinking.0: Splitting the solution into lines and finding where the error is
y-m-33-01.thinking.1: Examining whether being equal at one value is evidence that the expression is right
y-m-33-01.thinking.2: Choosing a way to check and testing the corrected result with that way
y-m-33-01.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-01.prereq.1: Able to look at the formula (a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ and write it (the formula is given in the material)
y-m-33-01.prereq.2: Calculating the value of an expression by plugging a number in for the letter x
y-m-33-01.prereq.3: Squaring negative numbers and the signs in multiplication
y-m-33-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line of Seojin's solution that contains a wrong calculation.
y-m-33-01.s.s1.hint.0: Redo the calculation of each line separately, line by line.
y-m-33-01.s.s1.hint.1: Where a negative number is inside parentheses, write down the sign before and after multiplying for each line and compare.
y-m-33-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is where it first went wrong. (−2)² is (−2)×(−2)=4, which is positive, but it was calculated as −4, so the coefficient of x became −12 instead of +12. Line 1 correctly plugged a=x, b=−2 into the formula, and the calculations in lines 2 and 4 are also right. Line 5 just carried over the result of the wrong line 3.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.prompt: You want to check by plugging numbers into x whether the result in line 5 is right. Choose all the values of x for which the value of the left side (x−2)³ and the value of Seojin's result x³ − 6x² − 12x − 8 become different, so that you can notice the error.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x = 1, 2, 0, −1 in turn into both expressions and write the two values in a table.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.hint.1: If there is an x where the values came out equal, think about whether being equal at that one value guarantees that the two expressions are equal as a whole.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.r.a: It is dangerous to believe it is right just because the two expressions came out equal at x=0. Being equal at one value is not evidence that the whole expressions are equal.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.r.b: At this value the two expressions come out different. This is a choice that knows checking by plugging in numbers can reveal the error.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.r.c: If you plug in this value, the left side is 0 and Seojin's result is not 0. You can notice the difference even when only one side becomes 0.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.r.d: Even when you plug in a negative number, calculating the values of the two expressions separately and comparing them shows the difference.
y-m-33-01.s.s2.explain: The corrected result x³ − 6x² + 12x − 8 and Seojin's result differ only in the coefficient of x, so the difference between the two expressions is 24x. So the same value comes out only at x = 0, and at every nonzero value they differ. Checking by plugging in numbers can reveal an error if you choose the values well, but you cannot conclude it is right from one value that came out equal.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Seojin. Include ① which line had what mistake, ② a way to check the result (such as plugging in numbers), and ③ the corrected result.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write (−2)² out as (−2)×(−2) and compare it with Seojin's value.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.hint.1: After writing the corrected result, pick one x value that revealed the error and test whether the left and right values are equal.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you recalculate just the line you pointed out to check that it really is the first wrong place?
y-m-33-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you examine whether the x value you used to check actually reveals the error?
y-m-33-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you test the corrected result again with the x value you chose?
y-m-33-01.s.s3.model.0: Seojin, in the 3rd line you calculated (−2)² as −4. (−2)²=(−2)×(−2)=4, so the coefficient of x should be 3·x·4=12. The corrected result is x³−6x²+12x−8. If you plug in x=1, the left side (1−2)³=−1 and the right side 1−6+12−8=−1 are equal, so it is confirmed.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.model.1: In the third line there is a sign mistake when squaring a negative number. Squaring a negative number gives a positive number, so (−2)² is 4, and calculating gives x³ − 6x² + 12x − 8. To see if it is right, I plug in x=2, and the left side is 0 and the right side 8−24+24−8 is also 0.
y-m-33-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another solution that chose x=2 as the check value.

y-m-33-02.title: If you know only one value, is the remainder determined?
y-m-33-02.topic: The remainder when divided by a quadratic expression and the information needed
y-m-33-02.goal: Show with several possible examples that the remainder when dividing by a quadratic expression cannot be determined when only one value is known, say what else must be known, and then actually find the remainder.
y-m-33-02.material: P(x) is a polynomial with real coefficients and its degree is not known. Only one fact is known so far: when P(x) is divided by x−1, the remainder is 3. Jiyun said, 'The remainder when P(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2) is 3,' and Hajun said, 'We can't tell with the current information.' Let Q(x) be the quotient and R(x) the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2). Then P(x) = (x−1)(x−2)Q(x) + R(x), and the degree of R(x) is less than 2. (How to read: P(x) is 'P of x', (x−1)(x−2) is 'x minus 1 times x minus 2')
y-m-33-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-33-02.thinking.1: Showing with several examples that it is not determined
y-m-33-02.thinking.2: Settling the conclusion with extra information and rebutting a wrong shortcut
y-m-33-02.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-02.prereq.1: The meaning of the quotient and remainder when a polynomial is divided by a polynomial: A = BQ + R and the degree of R is less than the degree of B
y-m-33-02.prereq.2: Finding the value by plugging a number into a polynomial
y-m-33-02.prereq.3: Solving a system of linear equations (two unknowns)
y-m-33-02.s.s1.prompt: What is the most appropriate judgment about whether R(x) can be found from only the information known now?
y-m-33-02.s.s1.hint.0: First write what form R(x) has and how many numbers in it need to be determined.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many equations the facts known now give for those numbers, and compare.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.o.a: It can be found. The remainder is 3
y-m-33-02.s.s1.r.a: This judgment treats the remainder 3 from dividing by x−1 as the same as the remainder R(x) from dividing by a quadratic expression. When the divisor changes, the form of the remainder changes too.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be found. We need to know the degree of P(x)
y-m-33-02.s.s1.r.b: Even without knowing the degree, the form of the remainder when dividing by a quadratic expression, degree 1 or lower, is fixed. You have not yet pinpointed exactly what information is needed.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.o.c: It cannot be found. We also need a value such as P(2)
y-m-33-02.s.s1.r.c: This judgment counts how many numbers in the remainder need to be determined and sees that the current information gives only part of them.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.o.d: It cannot be found. We need to know the quotient Q(x)
y-m-33-02.s.s1.r.d: Even without knowing the quotient, if you plug in an x that makes the quotient disappear, you can get an equation about the remainder. You did not see that the quotient is really needed.
y-m-33-02.s.s1.explain: R(x) has the form ax+b, so there are two numbers to determine, a and b. The only known fact is one equation in a+b, so R(x) cannot be determined yet. What is needed is not the degree or the quotient, but how much P is at another x value where the quotient disappears.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.prompt: R(x) = ax + b (a and b are integers from −5 to 8). Make 3 pairs (a, b), with different a, that do not contradict the known fact 'the remainder when divided by x−1 is 3'.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.hint.0: Look at which term becomes 0 when you plug x = 1 into P(x) = (x−1)(x−2)Q(x) + R(x).
y-m-33-02.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one a, adjust b to satisfy the known fact, and repeat the same process after changing a.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.var.a: Coefficient of x in the remainder
y-m-33-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a and b as integers from −5 to 8.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.ok.c2: It does not contradict the known fact.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.fail.c2: It contradicts the known fact (the value when x=1 is plugged in is 3). Check again what a+b should be.
y-m-33-02.s.s2.explain: P(1) = R(1) = a+b, so any pair with a+b=3 is possible. There are several pairs such as (0,3), (1,2), (2,1), so 'the information is lacking' is right. Jiyun's 'the remainder is 3' is just one of these, the case a=0.
y-m-33-02.s.s3.prompt: You now learn the additional fact that 'the remainder when P(x) is divided by x−2 is 5'. Write whether R(x) is now determined as one, what R(x) is if it is, and whether Jiyun's 'the remainder is 3' is right.
y-m-33-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write the equation you get by plugging in x = 2, showing how the new fact can be connected to R(x) = ax + b.
y-m-33-02.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many equations in a and b there are now, and find a and b from them.
y-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the equations connecting the values of P(1) and P(2) to R(x) each?
y-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check by plugging x = 1, 2 back into the R(x) you found to see that 3 and 5 come out?
y-m-33-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain why Jiyun's '3' differs from the R(x) you found?
y-m-33-02.s.s3.model.0: Plugging P(1)=3 and P(2)=5 into R(x)=ax+b gives a+b=3 and 2a+b=5, so a=2, b=1 and R(x)=2x+1. Jiyun's 'the remainder is 3' is only R(1)=3 and R(x) is not 3, so it is not right.
y-m-33-02.s.s3.model.1: With both values, R(x) is determined as one. In R(x)=ax+b, solving a+b=3 and 2a+b=5 as a system gives a=2, b=1. So the remainder is 2x+1, and Jiyun's statement that it is 3 is wrong.

y-m-33-03.title: How many values of x are enough to try?
y-m-33-03.topic: Properties of an identity: the number of values you need to check
y-m-33-03.goal: Judge from the evidence the condition (the degree of the expression) under which you can conclude an identity just from how many x values an equation holds for, and make a counterexample yourself.
y-m-33-03.material: a, b, and c are real constants, and you are told one at a time for which values of x the equation ax² + bx + c = 0 holds. What you want to know is whether you can conclude that this equation holds for all real values of x (an identity, that is, a = b = c = 0). The expression is a polynomial in x of degree 2 or lower. (How to read: ax² is 'a x squared', a = b = c = 0 is 'a, b, and c are all zero')
y-m-33-03.thinking.0: Adjusting how sure you are about a conclusion with limited evidence
y-m-33-03.thinking.1: Verifying a judgment by making a counterexample yourself
y-m-33-03.thinking.2: Explaining the condition for it to hold (the relationship between the degree and the number of values)
y-m-33-03.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-03.prereq.1: Coefficients and degree of a polynomial
y-m-33-03.prereq.2: Finding the value of an expression by plugging numbers in for letters
y-m-33-03.prereq.3: A system of linear equations with two unknowns
y-m-33-03.s.s1.prompt: Follow how your judgment changes each time one more value is revealed.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.hint.0: First imagine whether, besides a=b=c=0, there could be other (a, b, c) that hold for the values known so far.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the new information changes your first judgment, firms it up, or only adjusts how sure you are.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.info: We confirmed that the equation holds when we plug in x = 1 and also when we plug in x = 2.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we conclude that a = b = c = 0?
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The information that it holds for two values does not settle a = b = c = 0. The next action is to find yourself whether a nonzero (a, b, c) satisfies both conditions.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Yes. It held for two different values, so it is an identity
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment sees having two values as sufficient evidence. It has not yet considered how many numbers need to be determined in this expression.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Not yet known. We need to see whether a nonzero (a, b, c) is also possible
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment holds off on the conclusion and chooses to check whether there may be a counterexample.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Probably. It held for two values, so it is likely an identity
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment says it is not certain but does not look for whether there is a counterexample. It leaned toward the conclusion only from a feeling that it is likely.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.info: If we set (a, b, c) = (1, −3, 2), the equation holds at both x = 1 and x = 2. This (a, b, c) is not zero, and if you plug in x = 3, the value of the expression is 2.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: With this information, what happens to your first judgment?
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.after: (1, −3, 2) holds at x = 1, 2 but is not zero and does not hold at x = 3. So holding at two different values is not enough, and a third value can tell this example apart from a real identity.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: This example is a coincidence, so keep thinking that two values are enough
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment tries to protect the earlier idea even though a counterexample is right in front of you. One example breaks the claim that it is 'enough'.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We now have grounds that even if it holds at two values, we cannot call it an identity
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You sorted out your judgment by reflecting the fact that a nonzero example actually exists.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Two values are not enough, so we need to check at other x values too
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This judgment accepts the new information and decides what to test next.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: At x = 3 the value is 2, so this example does not hold at x = 1, 2 either
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You mixed up reading the value at x = 3 with whether it holds at x = 1, 2. You have to consider separately for each value whether it holds.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.info: This time we confirmed that it holds at all three values x = 1, 2, 3. The expression is still of degree 2 or lower.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Can we now conclude that a = b = c = 0?
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.after: If an expression of degree 2 or lower is 0 at three different values, then a = b = c = 0. But this conclusion is because the expression is of degree 2 or lower. For an expression of higher degree, three values may not be enough.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: No. It must hold at ten or more values before we can conclude
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You set the number of values large regardless of the degree of the expression. How many values are needed depends on what kind of expression it is.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: No. Even if it holds at three values, there must be a nonzero example
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This judgment sees the counterexample from the earlier step as still working. It did not reflect the point that that example broke at x = 3.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Yes. If an expression of degree 2 or lower holds at three values, then a=b=c=0
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This judgment draws the conclusion by connecting the degree and the number of values it holds for.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Yes. But this kind of conclusion is possible only when the expression is of degree 2 or lower
y-m-33-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This judgment states the conclusion together with the condition under which it holds.
y-m-33-03.s.s1.reflect: Whatever judgment you made at first, say whether the new information changed it or firmed it up. To conclude an identity, connect the point that the number of different values must be at least one more than the degree of the expression, with the point that a single counterexample breaks the claim that it is 'enough'.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 integer triples (a, b, c), with different a, for which ax² + bx + c = 0 holds at both x = 1 and x = 2 but a, b, c are not all 0. However, you cannot use the (1, −3, 2) seen above. All three numbers are from −20 to 20.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x = 1 and x = 2 each into ax² + bx + c and write two equations relating a, b, and c.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.hint.1: Test with the two equations whether you can make a similar example based on (1, −3, 2).
y-m-33-03.s.s2.ok.c1: All three numbers are integers within the range.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose the three numbers as integers from −20 to 20.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The value when x = 1 is plugged in is not 0.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The value when x = 2 is plugged in is not 0.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.ok.c4: None is 0 and it is not of the form (1, −3, 2).
y-m-33-03.s.s2.fail.c4: It is (0, 0, 0) or the (1, −3, 2) already seen.
y-m-33-03.s.s2.explain: If (a, b, c) = (k, −3k, 2k), it holds at both x = 1, 2. This expression equals the expansion of k(x−1)(x−2). So there are as many nonzero examples as you like, and this confirms that holding at two values alone does not make it an identity.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.prompt: Every expression that holds at x = 1, 2 has the form ax² + bx + c = a(x−1)(x−2). But we could not find a nonzero (a, b, c) that also holds at x = 3. What is the correct reason?
y-m-33-03.s.s3.hint.0: First calculate what value you get when you plug x = 3 into a(x−1)(x−2).
y-m-33-03.s.s3.hint.1: Then work out what a must be for that value to be 0, and what b and c become.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.o.a: If you plug in 3 or more values, any expression is an identity
y-m-33-03.s.s3.r.a: This generalization looks only at the number of values and does not consider the degree of the expression. For an expression of higher degree, three values may not be enough.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.o.b: We only tested integers and just missed the nonzero example
y-m-33-03.s.s3.r.b: This judgment blames limiting to integers. It did not check whether the same result comes out even if all real numbers are allowed.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.o.c: Because we did not use more varied ways of searching
y-m-33-03.s.s3.r.c: This judgment attributes not finding one only to a lack of method. It did not look for the reason in the structure of the expression.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.o.d: If x = 3, then 2a = 0, so a becomes 0
y-m-33-03.s.s3.r.d: This judgment plugs the new condition into the form a(x−1)(x−2) and determines the coefficient directly.
y-m-33-03.s.s3.explain: a(3−1)(3−2) = 2a, so to hold at x = 3, a = 0 is required, and then b = c = 0. This conclusion comes out because the expression is of degree 2 or lower. For an expression of degree 3 or higher, there are nonzero expressions that hold at the same three values.

y-m-33-04.title: What do we need to check to say there is no linear factor?
y-m-33-04.topic: Deciding on linear factors of a cubic expression (using the factor theorem)
y-m-33-04.goal: Compare and evaluate the factoring results obtained by different methods, find the gap in an argument that checked only some of the candidates, and say what checking is needed for the conclusion 'there is no factor' and the range in which that conclusion holds.
y-m-33-04.material: We look into whether a cubic expression with integer coefficients can be split into a product of linear expressions with integer coefficients. Mina solved P(x) = x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 by grouping the terms in pairs to find common factors, and got (x − 3)(x² − 4). Doyun used a method on the same expression: plug in the divisors of the constant term 12, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6, ±12, find the x where the value of P is 0, and get a linear factor. After that, we examine T(x) = x³ + 2x² + 3x + 4 with Doyun's method. (How to read: x³ is 'x cubed', ± is 'plus or minus')
y-m-33-04.thinking.0: Comparing and evaluating whether the results of two methods are the same
y-m-33-04.thinking.1: Spotting a conclusion drawn from insufficient evidence
y-m-33-04.thinking.2: Stating the range in which the conclusion holds (linear expressions with integer coefficients)
y-m-33-04.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-04.prereq.1: Finding the value of a cubic expression by plugging in numbers
y-m-33-04.prereq.2: Divisors of integers and expanding products
y-m-33-04.prereq.3: The meaning that if the remainder in a division is 0, the divisor is a factor
y-m-33-04.s.s1.prompt: The two people each carried their method all the way and split P(x) completely into a product of linear expressions with integer coefficients. Which is the correct explanation comparing the two results?
y-m-33-04.s.s1.hint.0: Assume each option is right, predict what calculation result should come out, and then calculate directly.
y-m-33-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write all the factors obtained by the two methods, and expand their product to compare whether it becomes P(x).
y-m-33-04.s.s1.o.a: Grouping gives (x−3)(x−2)(x+2), and plugging in values gives a different product
y-m-33-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment sees different methods as giving different factoring results. It did not consider what factors must come out for the product to be the same expression P.
y-m-33-04.s.s1.o.b: Plugging in values gets only (x−3), and the remaining quadratic expression cannot be divided
y-m-33-04.s.s1.r.b: This understands plugging in values as a method to use only once. It did not think about whether the same method can be used again on the quadratic expression.
y-m-33-04.s.s1.o.c: In both methods the factors are the same, x−3, x−2, x+2, and only the order differs
y-m-33-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment compares and evaluates that the two methods reach the same set of factors by different paths.
y-m-33-04.s.s1.o.d: Only the grouping method is right, and plugging in values cannot be used on a cubic expression
y-m-33-04.s.s1.r.d: This judgment sees only one method as correct. It did not check the basis for the method of plugging in values to find x where the value is 0.
y-m-33-04.s.s1.explain: The grouping method gives (x−3)(x²−4) = (x−3)(x−2)(x+2), and plugging in values gives the same three factors from P(3)=0, P(2)=0, P(−2)=0, or you can get one factor and then use it again on the remaining quadratic expression. The complete factorization with integer coefficients is the same regardless of the method, apart from the order of the product.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.prompt: This is Doyun's argument examining 'whether the linear expression x − k with integer coefficients is a factor' for T(x) = x³ + 2x² + 3x + 4. Choose the line whose basis is lacking.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.hint.0: Count all the candidates the 2nd line points to, and mark the candidates you checked in the 3rd line.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.hint.1: Plug one unmarked candidate into T(x) and find the value directly.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.line.0: For an integer k, if x − k is a factor of T(x), then T(k) = 0 must hold.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.line.1: The leading coefficient is 1, so k is a divisor of the constant term 4, that is, one of ±1, ±2, ±4.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.line.2: T(1) = 10 and T(−1) = 2, and both are not 0.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.line.3: Therefore T(x) has no linear factor of the form x − k.
y-m-33-04.s.s2.explain: It is the 4th line. Up to the 3rd line it is right. But the 2nd line points to 6 candidates, and what was actually checked is only 1 and −1. Since 2, −2, 4, −4 were not checked, you cannot say 'there is no linear factor'. The conclusion can be drawn only after testing all the candidates.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.prompt: Calculating the remaining candidates gave T(2) = 26, T(−2) = −2, T(4) = 112, T(−4) = −40. Together with the earlier T(1) and T(−1), what conclusion can you draw from these results within the range of integer coefficients?
y-m-33-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the T value for each of the 6 candidates in a table and look for any that is 0.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.hint.1: Test whether you can attach the phrase 'for linear expressions of what range' to the sentence of the conclusion.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.o.a: All 6 candidates are not 0, so there is no factor of the form x−k with integer coefficients
y-m-33-04.s.s3.r.a: This judgment reads the fact that all the candidates were checked together with the range of the conclusion.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.o.b: T(−2)=−2 is closest to 0, so x+2 is close to being a factor
y-m-33-04.s.s3.r.b: This reads a value close to 0 as meaning close to a factor. Deciding on a factor only asks whether the value is exactly 0.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.o.c: All the values are not 0, so T(x) cannot be factored in any range
y-m-33-04.s.s3.r.c: This conclusion goes beyond the range that was checked (linear expressions with integer coefficients). It did not consider what happens if the range of coefficients is widened.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.o.d: It is not 0 only for some of the candidates, so we cannot draw a conclusion yet
y-m-33-04.s.s3.r.d: You misjudged the range of candidates that were checked. By now all 6 candidates have been checked.
y-m-33-04.s.s3.explain: The T values are not 0 for all 6 candidates, so there is no linear factor x−k with integer coefficients. This conclusion is about linear expressions with integer coefficients. If real coefficients are also allowed, a cubic expression has a real root, so it can be split with a linear factor (though the root is not an integer).
y-m-33-04.s.s4.prompt: Write the conclusion about T(x) in one or two sentences, making clear which candidates the statement 'there is no factor' checked and in which range alone it holds.
y-m-33-04.s.s4.hint.0: Write in one line all the candidates you checked and whether any had a value of 0.
y-m-33-04.s.s4.hint.1: Put the range of coefficients before 'linear expression' and reread the sentence to see whether it is true.
y-m-33-04.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Can you write that you checked all the candidates without leaving any out?
y-m-33-04.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Is it clear what range of coefficients the linear expressions in 'there is no linear factor' have?
y-m-33-04.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the point that the conclusion may change if the range widens to the real numbers?
y-m-33-04.s.s4.model.0: I plugged in all the divisors of the constant term 4, ±1, ±2, ±4, and none of the T values is 0. So a linear expression x−k with integer coefficients is not a factor, and within the integers it cannot be split any further. If you open it up to the real numbers, it can be different.
y-m-33-04.s.s4.model.1: All 6 candidates were checked and there is no value that becomes 0. Therefore we can say there is no linear factor with integer coefficients. But this was said only in the range 'the coefficients are integers'.

y-m-33-05.title: How many cubic expressions are determined by two conditions?
y-m-33-05.topic: Finding undetermined coefficients with the factor theorem and the remainder theorem
y-m-33-05.goal: Compare the number of conditions with the number of unknowns to judge whether the solution is determined as one, make several expressions that fit the conditions, and design a condition yourself that determines the solution as one.
y-m-33-05.material: You want to make a cubic expression P(x) = x³ + ax² + bx + c. a, b, and c are integers, and both of the following conditions must be satisfied. (가) The remainder when P(x) is divided by x−2 is 0. (나) The remainder when P(x) is divided by x−1 is 4. (How to read: P(x) is 'P of x', ax² is 'a x squared')
y-m-33-05.thinking.0: Predicting the number of solutions by comparing the number of conditions and unknowns
y-m-33-05.thinking.1: Making and verifying several solutions that fit the conditions yourself
y-m-33-05.thinking.2: Designing a new condition that determines the solution as one
y-m-33-05.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-05.prereq.1: Finding the value of an expression by plugging numbers into a polynomial
y-m-33-05.prereq.2: Knowing that the remainder when divided by x−k is P(k) (or reading the explanation in the material)
y-m-33-05.prereq.3: Handling linear equations within the integers
y-m-33-05.s.s1.prompt: How many integer triples (a, b, c) satisfy both (가) and (나)? Judge by intuition before calculating.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.hint.0: First count how many unknowns there are and how many conditions.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether you can write (가) and (나) each as an equation in a, b, and c.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.r.a: I wonder whether you counted the situation of 3 unknowns and 2 conditions. You may not have compared the number of conditions and the number of unknowns.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.r.b: You cannot know whether the two conditions contradict each other before writing the equations. This judgment sees it as impossible without checking.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment sees that when there are fewer conditions than unknowns, the solution may not be determined as one.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.o.d: (가) and (나) say the same thing, so they are one condition
y-m-33-05.s.s1.r.d: The two conditions are information at different x values, but this judgment saw them as the same information.
y-m-33-05.s.s1.explain: Conditions (가) and (나) each give one linear equation in a, b, and c. There are 3 unknowns but 2 equations, so it is quite possible the solution is not determined as one. Make actual examples in the next step to check.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 triples (a, b, c), with different a, that satisfy both (가) and (나). a is an integer from −5 to 5, and b and c are integers from −40 to 40.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write as equations what value P becomes when you plug in what value of x for (가), and what value P is when you plug in what value for (나).
y-m-33-05.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one a first and find b and c that satisfy the two equations, then repeat the same process with another a.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, and c are integers within the range.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please check that a, b, and c are integers within the range.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not satisfy (가). Check the value of P when you plug in the right value for x.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.fail.c3: It does not satisfy (나). Check the value of P when you plug in the right value for x.
y-m-33-05.s.s2.explain: If b = −11 − 3a and c = 14 + 2a, then whatever integer a is, both (가) and (나) are satisfied. For example, if a=0, P(x)=x³−11x+14. There are 2 conditions and 3 unknowns, so several solutions arise.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.prompt: We want to add a condition (다) to (가) and (나) so that the integer triple (a, b, c) is determined as one. Choose all the suitable (다).
y-m-33-05.s.s3.hint.0: Connect each option to b = −11−3a and c = 14+2a and test how many a are left.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.hint.1: Look for an option that repeats information that already came from (가) or (나).
y-m-33-05.s.s3.r.a: This is a condition already in (가). It restates the same information, so it does not narrow the solution further.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.r.b: You chose a condition that adds information at a new x value so that there are three equations.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.r.c: If (가) and (나) are satisfied, c is already even. It is not a new restriction.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.r.d: You narrowed the solution by adding information at an x value not used in (가) and (나).
y-m-33-05.s.s3.r.e: An inequality can narrow the solution but cannot determine it as one. There are still several integers a in this range.
y-m-33-05.s.s3.explain: With (다) P(0)=6, c=6, and from c=14+2a we get a=−4, b=1. P(3)=0 gives 8+2a=0, so a=−4. P(2)=0 is the same as (가), and the condition that c is even is not new information because c=14+2a is already even. a>1 does not determine the solution as one. Comparing conditions like this is what choosing a 'sufficient condition' means.
y-m-33-05.s.s4.prompt: Choose and write a (다) yourself, and show in two or three lines the process by which a, b, and c are all determined by that condition. (It may be a condition not in the options above.)
y-m-33-05.s.s4.hint.0: Connect (다) to the equations b = −11−3a, c = 14+2a and find a first.
y-m-33-05.s.s4.hint.1: After getting a, find b and then c in turn, and plug the three numbers into P(x) to check (가), (나), and (다) once each.
y-m-33-05.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the (다) you made really determines the solution as one (that two or more are not left)?
y-m-33-05.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you plug the a, b, and c you found into all of (가), (나), and (다)?
y-m-33-05.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Is your (다) not a repeat of (가) or (나)?
y-m-33-05.s.s4.model.0: Say (다) is P(0)=6. Then c=6. Then 14+2a=6 gives a=−4, and b=−11−3a=1. So P(x)=x³−4x²+x+6.
y-m-33-05.s.s4.model.1: Say (다) is a=1. Then b=−14 and c=16, so P(x)=x³+x²−14x+16 is determined as one.

y-m-33-06.title: The same expression, different 'quotients and remainders'?
y-m-33-06.topic: The identity A=BQ+R of polynomial division and the condition on the degree of the remainder
y-m-33-06.goal: Confirm by making them yourself that there can be several equations of the form A = BQ + R, and explain that a condition on the degree of the remainder is needed for the quotient and remainder of a division to be determined as one.
y-m-33-06.material: A(x) = x³ + 2x + 1 and B(x) = x² + 1. Jiho wrote A(x) = B(x)·x + (x + 1), and Soeun wrote A(x) = B(x)·(x + 1) + (−x² + x). Both say they found 'the quotient and remainder when A is divided by B'. (How to read: A(x) is 'A of x', B(x)·x is 'B of x times x')
y-m-33-06.thinking.0: Verifying by comparing coefficients whether an identity holds
y-m-33-06.thinking.1: Showing with examples that without a condition there are several solutions
y-m-33-06.thinking.2: Explaining the condition needed for uniqueness
y-m-33-06.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-06.prereq.1: Expanding products of polynomials and combining like terms
y-m-33-06.prereq.2: The condition for two polynomials to be equal: the coefficients of the same degree are equal
y-m-33-06.prereq.3: The form of the result of dividing a polynomial by a polynomial, A = BQ + R
y-m-33-06.s.s1.prompt: After expanding the two equations to check, choose the most appropriate judgment.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.hint.0: Expand the right side of each equation, combine like terms, and compare the coefficients with A.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each equation, write the degree of the remainder and compare it with the degree of B.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.o.a: Both hold, so both are accepted as the quotient and remainder
y-m-33-06.s.s1.r.a: This accepted them as the result of a division only by seeing whether the equation holds. It did not examine the form of the remainder.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.o.b: Soeun's equation is wrong because when expanded it differs from A
y-m-33-06.s.s1.r.b: You may have judged it by the shape looking different, without actually comparing the expansion results. When expanded, it equals A.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.o.c: Jiho's equation is wrong because when expanded it differs from A
y-m-33-06.s.s1.r.c: This may be a judgment made without checking the expansion calculation. When expanded, it equals A.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.o.d: Both hold, but we also need to examine the degree of the remainder
y-m-33-06.s.s1.r.d: This judgment separates whether the equation holds from whether it is the result of a division, as different questions.
y-m-33-06.s.s1.explain: B·x + (x+1) = x³+x+x+1 = x³+2x+1, and B·(x+1) + (−x²+x) = x³+x²+x+1−x²+x = x³+2x+1. Both are identities. But to accept them as the quotient and remainder, you must also examine whether the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of B (2).
y-m-33-06.s.s2.prompt: Set Q(x) = x + q (q is an integer from −3 to 3), and find the integer coefficients u, v, w of R(x) = ux² + vx + w so that A(x) = B(x)·Q(x) + R(x) becomes an identity. Make 3 examples with different q.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the expanded form of B(x)·(x + q) and subtract it from A(x).
y-m-33-06.s.s2.hint.1: Changing q one at a time, write in a table how u, v, and w change.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.var.u: Coefficient u of x² in R
y-m-33-06.s.s2.var.v: Coefficient v of x in R
y-m-33-06.s.s2.ok.c1: q is an integer within the range.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose q as an integer from −3 to 3.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The x² coefficient is different. Recheck the x² term of the expression A minus B·Q.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The x coefficient is different. Recheck the x term of the expression A minus B·Q.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The constant term is different. Recheck the constant term of the expression A minus B·Q.
y-m-33-06.s.s2.explain: R = A − B(x+q) = −q·x² + x + (1−q). If q=0, R=x+1 (Jiho), and if q=1, R=−x²+x (Soeun). Even if q changes, the equation holds as long as R is matched, so there are several equations of the form A = BQ + R.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.r.a: This is a judgment that did not check what happens to the x² coefficient of R for positive q. Look at the case where u=−q becomes 0.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.r.b: This judgment found the case where the x² coefficient of R disappears and compared the degrees.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.r.c: You did not consider whether the x² coefficient is nonzero for negative q too.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.r.d: This judgment sees the degree of R as not changing even if q changes. Compare the expressions for R that you made.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.explain: The x² coefficient of R is −q. Only when q=0 does this coefficient become 0, so R becomes x+1 (degree 1), which is less than the degree 2 of B. For other q, R is of degree 2, so it is not accepted as the remainder of a division.
y-m-33-06.s.s4.prompt: Write, using Jiho's and Soeun's solutions or the examples you just made as evidence, why a condition like 'degree of the remainder < degree of the divisor' is needed for the quotient and remainder of a division to be 'determined as one'.
y-m-33-06.s.s4.hint.0: Count how many pairs of quotient and remainder were made from the same A and B when there is no condition.
y-m-33-06.s.s4.hint.1: Find, among the examples you made, the pair that remains when the condition is applied.
y-m-33-06.s.s4.selfAssess.0: In the examples you gave, is it clear that the same A and B have different quotients and remainders?
y-m-33-06.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you explain with the examples you made why only one remains when the condition is applied?
y-m-33-06.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you write the reason in your own words, without memorizing the name of the condition?
y-m-33-06.s.s4.model.0: Just writing in the form A=B·Q+R lets you make several pairs by changing q. Jiho's remainder is x+1, degree 1, and Soeun's is −x²+x, degree 2. If you set the condition that the degree of the remainder is less than the degree 2 of B, only Jiho's pair remains, so the quotient and remainder are determined as one.
y-m-33-06.s.s4.model.1: Without a condition, even if you change Q as in q=0, 1, 2, the equation holds as long as R is matched, so many pairs arise. So you must limit the degree of the remainder to less than that of B for only q=0 to remain.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.prompt: If you change q to every integer from −3 to 3, for which values of q does the degree of R(x) become lower than the degree of B(x)?
y-m-33-06.s.s3.hint.0: Change q in a few ways, write R(x), and write down the degree of each.
y-m-33-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write down which coefficient of R must be what for the degree of R to be lower than B's degree, 2, and find the q that makes that happen.

y-m-33-07.title: Is this solution finished? Writing a message to send to a friend
y-m-33-07.topic: Factoring a quartic expression using substitution and judging completion
y-m-33-07.goal: Compare the form the problem asks for (a product of linear expressions) with the result of the solution to judge whether the solution is finished, and write a message that helps a friend fix it by themselves without giving the answer.
y-m-33-07.material: A friend solved the following problem and wrote 'Done!'. Problem: Write (x² + x)² − 8(x² + x) + 12 as a product of linear expressions with integer coefficients. The friend's solution is the four lines below. This is a task where you write by yourself words that will help the friend finish the solution on their own. (How to read: (x² + x)² is 'open parenthesis, x squared plus x, close parenthesis, squared')
y-m-33-07.thinking.0: Judging whether a solution is complete by comparing what the problem asks for with the form of the result
y-m-33-07.thinking.1: Telling apart helpful feedback from feedback that is not
y-m-33-07.thinking.2: Writing a message that guides the next action without writing the answer
y-m-33-07.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-07.prereq.1: Factoring a quadratic expression (using sum and product)
y-m-33-07.prereq.2: Handling an expression in which part of it is replaced by one letter
y-m-33-07.prereq.3: Reading the form the problem asks for
y-m-33-07.s.s1.prompt: In the friend's solution, choose the line whose conclusion does not match what the problem asks for.
y-m-33-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put the form the problem asks for and the degrees in the result of the 3rd line side by side and compare.
y-m-33-07.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one parenthesis in the 3rd line and try plugging in a few integer values to see whether any makes it 0.
y-m-33-07.s.s1.line.0: Letting x² + x = t, the given expression is t² − 8t + 12.
y-m-33-07.s.s1.line.2: Changing t back to x² + x gives (x² + x − 2)(x² + x − 6).
y-m-33-07.s.s1.line.3: It has become a product, so the factoring is finished.
y-m-33-07.s.s1.explain: It is the 4th line. The problem said to write it as a 'product of linear expressions', but the two parentheses in the 3rd line are still quadratic expressions. The quadratic x²+x−2 is 0 at x=1 and x²+x−6 is 0 at x=2, so each can be split further. The calculations themselves in lines 1 to 3 are all right.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose the most helpful message to send to the friend. (Use as the criterion helping the friend fix it by themselves rather than telling them the answer.)
y-m-33-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each message, write in one line what the friend who receives it will do next.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether the message separates the part that is right from the part that remains.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.o.a: The answer is (x−1)(x+2)(x−2)(x+3). Rewrite it with this
y-m-33-07.s.s2.r.a: Giving the answer is fast, but the friend loses the chance to find out for themselves where it was not finished. This choice sets the standard of help at 'getting it right right now'.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.o.b: The 4th line is wrong. Solve it again from the start
y-m-33-07.s.s2.r.b: This only tells them it is wrong and does not say what to check. It also puts on them the burden of redoing lines 1 to 3, which were already right.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.o.c: Look at whether the parentheses in the 3rd line are linear, and if not, split them further
y-m-33-07.s.s2.r.c: This guides the action of comparing what the problem asks for with the form of the result.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.o.d: Substitution is confusing, so don't use it; expand and solve it
y-m-33-07.s.s2.r.d: This advised changing a method that was used correctly. It is a choice that did not look at how far the friend's solution was right.
y-m-33-07.s.s2.explain: Good feedback acknowledges the part that is right and tells what still remains and a way to check it on their own. c guides an action to check, a gives the answer, b just says to redo it with no direction, and d tells them to throw away a method that is right.
y-m-33-07.s.s3.prompt: Write the message to send to the friend yourself. Include ① what is still not done in the current solution and ② one way the friend can check on their own, but ③ do not write the completed answer expression.
y-m-33-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write a sentence that points out one right line in the friend's solution and acknowledges it.
y-m-33-07.s.s3.hint.1: Then write one action the friend can try on a parenthesis in the 3rd line (such as which values to plug in).
y-m-33-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the message have words that acknowledge the part the friend did right?
y-m-33-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can the friend tell what to do next just from reading the message?
y-m-33-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the direction clear without giving away the answer?
y-m-33-07.s.s3.model.0: You said you were done at the 4th line, but the two parentheses in the 3rd line are still quadratic expressions. The problem wants a product of linear expressions, so you need to see whether each parenthesis can be split further. Plug an integer such as x=1 or x=2 into a parenthesis and check whether it becomes 0.
y-m-33-07.s.s3.model.1: You did great substituting and solving with t! But it is not yet a product of linear expressions. See whether a parenthesis like x²+x−2 can be factored once more using the sum and product of two numbers.

y-m-33-08.title: If you combine two expressions of the same degree, what happens to the degree?
y-m-33-08.topic: Degree of the sum and product of polynomials
y-m-33-08.goal: Examine claims about the degree of the sum and product of two cubic expressions, make a counterexample yourself where the sum is not a cubic expression, and write what is always true and the condition for it to hold.
y-m-33-08.material: A(x) and B(x) are cubic expressions with real coefficients (that is, the coefficient of x³ is not 0). Sua said, 'A + B is always a cubic expression,' and Yunho said, 'The product A·B of A and B is always a degree-6 expression.' Let's examine whether the two statements are always true. (How to read: x³ is 'x cubed', A·B is 'A times B')
y-m-33-08.thinking.0: Telling apart true claims and false claims
y-m-33-08.thinking.1: Making a counterexample yourself and verifying it with a condition
y-m-33-08.thinking.2: Telling apart statements that are always true and conditional statements
y-m-33-08.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-08.prereq.1: Degree and leading coefficient of a polynomial
y-m-33-08.prereq.3: How a counterexample breaks a claim
y-m-33-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the correct statements below.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.hint.0: Choose two simple cubic expressions yourself and write the degree of the sum and of the product.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.hint.1: Test whether the sum might not be a cubic expression, and what happens if you add the leading terms.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.o.a: The degree of A + B cannot be greater than 3
y-m-33-08.s.s1.r.a: This choice counted how the degree is limited in the sum of two expressions.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.o.b: A − B is always a quadratic expression
y-m-33-08.s.s1.r.b: This judgment sees the degree as dropping by one step when you take the difference. What happens if you think about the case where the leading terms of A and B are not the same?
y-m-33-08.s.s1.o.c: The degree of A·B is always 6
y-m-33-08.s.s1.r.c: This choice looked at the leading terms being multiplied together.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.o.d: The degree of A + B is 3 + 3 = 6
y-m-33-08.s.s1.r.d: This mixed up the sum and the product and added the degrees. In a sum, the degrees do not add.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.o.e: There are cases where A + B is not a cubic expression
y-m-33-08.s.s1.r.e: This choice doubted Sua's 'always' and thought of the possibility of a counterexample.
y-m-33-08.s.s1.explain: The degree of a sum is 3 or less (the leading term can disappear). A product is always degree 6, because the product of the leading coefficients is not 0 (for real coefficients). A − B can also be cubic or lower, so it is not 'always quadratic'. It is also wrong to add the degrees of a sum as you do for a product.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.prompt: Set A = a₃x³ + a₂x² and B = b₃x³ + b₂x² (a₃ and b₃ are not 0). Make 2 different examples where A + B is not a cubic expression but exactly a quadratic expression. All coefficients are integers from −9 to 9, and A and B swapped count as the same example. (Input names: a3, a2, b3, b2)
y-m-33-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the coefficient of x³ and the coefficient of x² in A + B.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.hint.1: Write separately what the coefficient of x³ must be for the sum not to be cubic, and what the coefficient of x² must be for it to be quadratic.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The four numbers are integers within the range.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose the four numbers as integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.ok.c2: A and B are both cubic expressions.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.fail.c2: A and B must both be cubic expressions, so the coefficient of x³ cannot be 0.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The x³ term disappears in the sum.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The x³ term does not disappear in the sum. Check the sum of the x³ coefficients.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The sum is exactly a quadratic expression.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The x² coefficient of the sum is also 0, so it is not a quadratic expression.
y-m-33-08.s.s2.explain: If the sum of the x³ coefficients is 0, the cubic term disappears in A+B, and if the sum of the x² coefficients is not 0, the degree is exactly 2. Even one such example breaks Sua's 'always'.
y-m-33-08.s.s3.prompt: Fix Sua's statement: write what is always true about the degree of A + B, and also write the condition for A + B to be a cubic expression.
y-m-33-08.s.s3.hint.0: In the examples you made earlier, sum up in terms of the sum of the x³ coefficients why the degree of A + B could not be 3.
y-m-33-08.s.s3.hint.1: Test once more whether the statement that always holds has no counterexample.
y-m-33-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the sentence you wrote is always true with no counterexample?
y-m-33-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the condition for being a cubic expression linked to the sum of the x³ coefficients?
y-m-33-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you sort out your own thinking about Yunho's statement (the product is always degree 6) separately?
y-m-33-08.s.s3.model.0: The degree of A+B is 3 or less. It is a cubic expression only when the sum of the x³ coefficients is not 0, and if it is 0, the degree is lower.
y-m-33-08.s.s3.model.1: What is always true is 'the degree of A+B does not exceed 3'. If the sum of the cubic-term coefficients of the two expressions is not 0, it is a cubic expression, and if it adds up to 0, the leading term disappears and the degree is lower than 3.

y-m-33-09.title: Can we trust a value found from a sum and a sum of squares?
y-m-33-09.topic: Variations of the multiplication formula: sum and product, and the condition for real numbers to exist
y-m-33-09.goal: Notice that a value found using a variation of the multiplication formula may come out formally even though such real numbers may not exist, and find and explain by yourself the condition for them to exist.
y-m-33-09.material: Two pieces of information are given for real numbers a and b: a + b = 4 and a² + b² = 6. Minjae wants to find the value of a³ + b³ from this information. (How to read: a² + b² is 'a squared plus b squared')
y-m-33-09.thinking.0: Finding a value using a variation of the multiplication formula
y-m-33-09.thinking.1: Telling apart that a calculation result came out from that numbers satisfying the conditions exist
y-m-33-09.thinking.2: Setting up the condition for existence yourself and explaining it
y-m-33-09.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-09.prereq.1: Using the multiplication formula (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
y-m-33-09.prereq.2: Able to look at and write a variation of (a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³
y-m-33-09.prereq.3: The fact that the square of a real number is 0 or more
y-m-33-09.s.s1.prompt: Using a variation of the multiplication formula, what is the value of a³ + b³?
y-m-33-09.s.s1.hint.0: Plug the given values into the expanded form of (a+b)² and find ab first.
y-m-33-09.s.s1.hint.1: In the expanded form of (a+b)³, write the a³+b³ part and the remaining part separately.
y-m-33-09.s.s1.r.a: This calculation treats the value of (a+b)³ as a³+b³ directly. The middle term 3ab(a+b) is missing.
y-m-33-09.s.s1.r.b: This calculation subtracts only 3ab without multiplying by (a+b) in 3ab(a+b).
y-m-33-09.s.s1.r.c: This is the result of finding ab first and then calculating the sum of cubes using the sum and product.
y-m-33-09.s.s1.r.d: This is a result calculated by putting the value of a²+b² in the place of ab. The roles of the sum and the product got swapped.
y-m-33-09.s.s1.explain: From (a+b)² = a²+b²+2ab, 16 = 6 + 2ab, so ab = 5. Then a³+b³ = (a+b)³ − 3ab(a+b) = 64 − 3·5·4 = 4.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.prompt: Choose the line in Minjae's solution whose basis is lacking.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.hint.0: Recalculate each line one at a time to check that its calculation is right.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.line.0: (a+b)² = 16, and this is a² + b² + 2ab, so 16 = 6 + 2ab, that is, ab = 5.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.line.3: Therefore there are real numbers a and b whose sum is 4 and whose sum of squares is 6, and the sum of their cubes is 4.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.explain: It is the 4th line. The first three lines are all calculated correctly. But in the 3rd line (a−b)² came out as −4, and the square of a real number is 0 or more. So there are no real numbers a and b that satisfy the conditions. The value 4 is only a formal calculation result under the assumption that such real numbers exist.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.prompt: Keep a + b = 4 as it is and change only the value of a² + b². Depending on that value, real numbers a and b satisfying the conditions may or may not exist. Choose all the values for which real numbers a and b exist.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.hint.0: Fix one value from the options and calculate ab and (a−b)² in turn.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.hint.1: Find in the table the value where the sign of (a−b)² changes.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.r.a: You may have chosen it because it is close to 6 without finding ab and (a−b)². If you check, (a−b)² becomes negative.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.r.b: You chose it after checking that (a−b)² is 0 or more.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.r.c: You chose it after finding (a−b)² and checking that it is greater than 0.
y-m-33-09.s.s3.r.d: You missed the point that existence becomes harder as the value gets smaller. You can tell by checking (a−b)².
y-m-33-09.s.s3.explain: Letting a²+b²=s, ab=(16−s)/2 and (a−b)² = s − 2ab = 2s − 16. For this value to be 0 or more, s ≥ 8 is needed. 8 and 10 are possible (8 with a=b=2), and for 7 and 5, (a−b)² is negative, so they are impossible.
y-m-33-09.s.s4.prompt: Explain how large a² + b² must be at least for real numbers a and b with sum 4 to exist, and how you can find that criterion. Also include why the original problem (a² + b² = 6) was a problem.
y-m-33-09.s.s4.hint.0: Write (a−b)² as an expression in a² + b² and connect it to the condition that it is 0 or more.
y-m-33-09.s.s4.hint.1: Plug the value 6 from the original problem into that expression and check the sign of the result.
y-m-33-09.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Does the process of finding the criterion include expressions such as ab and (a−b)²?
y-m-33-09.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you test the criterion directly on values such as 6, 8, and 10 to check it?
y-m-33-09.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you explain the difference between a formal value and numbers that actually exist?
y-m-33-09.s.s4.model.0: If a and b are real, (a−b)² is 0 or more, but if a²+b²=6, then (a−b)²=6−2·5=−4, which is negative, so such real numbers do not exist. For (a−b)²=2(a²+b²)−16 to be 0 or more, a²+b² must be 8 or more.
y-m-33-09.s.s4.model.1: ab=(16−s)/2, and if a and b are real, the discriminant must be 0 or more. If a²+b²=6, the discriminant is −4, so there are no real numbers, and they exist only when a²+b² is 8 or more.
y-m-33-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the value calculated in each line matches the properties of real numbers, and whether the statement in the last line really follows from the results of the earlier lines.

y-m-33-10.title: The quotient and remainder when dividing by 2x−1: checking this solution
y-m-33-10.topic: Synthetic division and division by a linear expression whose coefficient is not 1
y-m-33-10.goal: Analyze what stays the same and what changes when moving the result of dividing by x−1/2 to the result of dividing by 2x−1, and make several expressions that satisfy the remainder condition.
y-m-33-10.material: A student who wanted to find the quotient and remainder when dividing P(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + x − 5 by 2x − 1 used synthetic division and solved it as follows. (How to read: 2x³ is '2 x cubed', 2x−1 is '2x minus 1', 1/2 is 'one half')
y-m-33-10.thinking.0: Checking whether the final conclusion of the solution really follows from the earlier calculations
y-m-33-10.thinking.1: Analyzing the relationship between the quotient and remainder when the same expression is divided by different linear expressions
y-m-33-10.thinking.2: Making and verifying several expressions that fit a condition
y-m-33-10.prereq.0: The H2 in this set is only a difficulty and support level in the production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: the student has learned middle school multiplication formulas and factoring and calculations with linear and quadratic expressions, and has just encountered the polynomial unit of high school Common Math.
y-m-33-10.prereq.1: How to find the quotient and remainder when dividing by x−k using synthetic division
y-m-33-10.prereq.2: The division equation A = BQ + R
y-m-33-10.s.s1.prompt: In the student's solution, choose the line that contains a conclusion that does not come from the earlier lines.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write what the divisor is in the 3rd line and in the 4th line, and compare them.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write the division equation P(x) = (divisor) × (quotient) + remainder using the result of the 3rd line, then rewrite the divisor as 2x − 1.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.line.0: From 2x − 1 = 0, x = 1/2, so we do synthetic division with 1/2.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.line.1: With coefficients 2, −3, 1, −5, the bottom row becomes 2, −2, 0, −5.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.line.2: So the quotient when P(x) is divided by x − 1/2 is 2x² − 2x and the remainder is −5.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.line.3: That is, the quotient when P(x) is divided by 2x − 1 is 2x² − 2x and the remainder is −5.
y-m-33-10.s.s1.explain: It is the 4th line. The calculations in lines 1 to 3 are right. The quotient 2x²−2x obtained by synthetic division is the quotient when dividing by x−1/2. You have to factor out the 2, as in P(x) = (x−1/2)(2x²−2x) − 5 = (2x−1)(x²−x) − 5, to get the quotient when dividing by 2x−1. The remainder −5 is the same in both cases.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the correct explanations comparing dividing the same P(x) by x − 1/2 and by 2x − 1.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.hint.0: In P = (x−1/2)Q + R, write which number moves where when you rewrite (x−1/2) as (2x−1).
y-m-33-10.s.s2.hint.1: After moving it, compare what goes in the place of the quotient and remainder.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.o.a: The quotients in the two cases are the same
y-m-33-10.s.s2.r.a: This judgment sees the quotients as the same even though the divisors are different. In the equation P = BQ + R, check what happens to Q when B is different.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.o.b: The remainders in the two cases are the same
y-m-33-10.s.s2.r.b: This choice considered why the remainder does not change even when the form of the divisor changes.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.o.c: The remainder when dividing by 2x−1 becomes half
y-m-33-10.s.s2.r.c: This judgment sees the remainder as being divided along with the quotient. It did not examine where the remainder is determined.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.o.d: The quotient when dividing by 2x−1 becomes half
y-m-33-10.s.s2.r.d: This choice read the relationship between the number multiplied into the divisor and the quotient.
y-m-33-10.s.s2.explain: P = (x−1/2)·Q + R = (2x−1)·(Q/2) + R, so the quotient when dividing by 2x−1 is Q/2 and the remainder R does not change. Here Q = 2x²−2x, so Q/2 = x²−x.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.prompt: Make a cubic expression P(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d (a, b, c, d are integers from −9 to 9, and a is not 0) so that the remainder when P(x) is divided by 2x − 1 is 3. Make 3 different expressions.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how you can rewrite 'the remainder is 3' as the value of P at some value of x.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.hint.1: First fix some of a, b, c, d, then determine the remaining letters to fit the condition.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.ok.c1: The four numbers are integers within the range.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.fail.c1: Please choose the four numbers as integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.fail.c2: If the coefficient a of x³ is 0, it is not a cubic expression.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.ok.c3: The remainder when divided by 2x−1 is 3.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.fail.c3: The remainder is not 3. Check whether the value of P at the x that makes 2x−1=0 is 3.
y-m-33-10.s.s3.explain: The remainder when divided by 2x−1 is P(1/2) = a/8 + b/4 + c/2 + d, and this is 3, so multiplying both sides by 8 gives the condition a + 2b + 4c + 8d = 24. There are several integer quadruples that satisfy this condition. For example, for (4, 2, 4, 0), P(1/2) = 1/2 + 1/2 + 2 + 0 = 3.
